newsitem.title: USA: Philippine president urges U.S. on extradition.
newsitem.headline: Philippine president urges U.S. on extradition.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos called on Washington on Wednesday to live up to a new extradition treaty and hand over a woman living in San Francisco wanted in a multimillion dollar securities fraud in the Philippines.
Ramos, who was heading a trade-delegation to California, also urged the United States to fulfil its promises to Filipinos who fought in the U.S. armed forces during the Second World War.
Asked at a news conference about the recently concluded U.S.-Philippine extradition treaty, Ramos said the agreement had been ratified by the Philippine legislature.

"In fact, the agreement is being tested now -- we are asking for the extradition of a woman involved in a big bank fraud," he said. He said the woman, identified by aides as Marilyn Nite, was living in San Francisco.
"We have begun to implement it on our side, the United States must now do its part," said Ramos.
He acknowledged the situation had been complicated somewhat by the fact that Nite had married an American.

An aide later explained that Nite was wanted on an outstanding 1995 warrant accusing her of economic sabotage connected to a multimillion dollar fraud at the securities firm Bancap at which she was a senior official.
No further details of the case were immediately available.
In a wide-ranging news conference at the Los Angeles City Hall, Ramos was also asked about the status of Philippine Second World War veterans.

"Filipino veterans who served in the U.S. Army were promised everything while they were fighting -- justice, just like other GI's for defending the Pacific," he said. "But they did not get that from the United States."
However, he said, "there is growing momentum in (the U.S.) Congress of support for them."
He was referring to the Filipino Veterans Equity Bill which is still in the early stages of committee debate in both the Senate and the House of Representatives.
Under the bill, Philippine veterans would be granted the same pension, benefits and health care given American military veterans.
"There are about 75,000 of them. They are getting older and weaker and many are probably not going to survive longer on this Earth," said Ramos. "We are hoping and praying for them."

Later Wednesday Ramos met with California Gov. Pete Wilson and also had talks with California business leaders. After three days in Los Angeles and San Diego, Ramos was scheduled to continue his tour in Mexico on Friday.

The Philippine president told reporters that since arriving in Los Angeles on Tuesday, his team had reached agreement on at least seven joint ventures between his country and U.S. firms -- many of them in the high-tehcnology field.
"California is on the cutting edge of the industry of the future -- an industry the Philippines wants to join," he said.
One business leader Ramos met was a Disney senior official involved in developing resorts, theme parks and rides.
Asked if there was a possibiity of a Disneyland in the Philippines' future, Ramos laughed and said there had been discussions with several companies about building theme parks.
"My grandchildren would love it," he said.
